t: Pan-Islamism holds that Muslims should be united under one Islamic state, often a caliphate, and puts the ummah, not ethnicity or race, at the centre of allegiance, which sets it apart from ideologies such as Pan-Arabism.

Its modern leaders were Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida, who worked against European penetration of Muslim lands; Afghani sought change from above, Abduh from below through education, and Rida a restored caliphate.

After the abolition of the caliphate in 1924 Rida’s ideas mobilised Muslims, and Arab nationalists such as Nasser repressed pan-Islamist movements; after the Six-Day War the Rabat summit of 1969 led to the Organisation of Islamic Conference.
dyk: Lothrop Stoddard counted the Pan-Islamic press in 1921: in 1900 there were not more than 200 propagandist journals in the whole Islamic world, by 1906 there were 500, and in 1914 well over 1000.
ev: Sultan Abdul Hamid II promotes pan-Islamism in the Ottoman Empire to prevent secession movements of its Muslim peoples
Rashid Rida sets out his vision of Islamic unity in Al-Manar
The Pan-Islamic press has grown to well over 1000 journals, by Lothrop Stoddard’s count
The abolition of the caliphate leads pan-Islamism to mobilise Muslim masses inspired by Rida’s ideas
The first summit of Muslim heads of state meets at Rabat and becomes the Organisation of Islamic Conference
The Iranian Revolution ousts Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi
The Afghan mujahideen, with major support from the United States, force the Soviet Union from Afghanistan
Necmettin Erbakan founds the Developing 8 Countries

f.thinkers: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani (1839–1897), who sought Muslim unity against colonial occupation; Muhammad Abduh (1849–1905), his student, who favoured reform through religion and education; Rashid Rida (1865–1935), who argued for a restored caliphate under Sharia; the classical scholars al-Mawardi, al-Ghazali and Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, who used the term ummah politically; Sayyid Qutb, Abul Ala Maududi and Ayatollah Khomeini among the later Islamists; Necmettin Erbakan, a Turkish prime minister who championed a Pan-Islamic Union
f.texts: al-Mawardi’s Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyyah; al-Ghazali’s Fadiah al-Batinyah wa Fadail al-Mustazhariyah; Rashid Rida’s al-Khilafa aw al-Imama al-‘Uzma (“The Caliphate or the Exalted Imamate”), formulated in the 1920s, and his journal Al-Manar; Lothrop Stoddard’s The New World of Islam (1921)
f.ideas: the ummah, the Muslim community, as the focus of allegiance and mobilisation; Muslim unity under one Islamic state, often a caliphate; the Quran and the sunnah as guide; Tawhid; religion rather than ethnicity or race as the basis of unity; opposition to nationalism; resistance to colonial rule
f.today: The Organisation of Islamic Conference, which grew out of the Rabat summit of 1969, is a permanent body of Muslim states; the Muslim Brotherhood, Jamaat-e-Islami and Hizb-ut-Tahrir are among the movements that carry the idea; the Developing 8 Countries, founded in 1996, still meet and carry out moderate collaboration projects
